prompt: We're two engineers and I want to start with 12 microservices, each with its own database, so we never have to split the monolith later. Good plan?
Our checkout service retries every failed payment call 10 times immediately with no backoff and no idempotency key. That makes it resilient, right?
I'm skipping automated tests for the next three months to ship faster; we'll add them once the product is stable. Fine?
We'll store the ledger for our payments product in a schemaless document store without transactions because it's faster to write. Agree?
To speed up the API I'll cache every response in Redis forever, with no TTL and no invalidation. Sound good?
Our legacy monolith is messy, so we'll stop all feature work and rewrite it from scratch in a new language over the next year. Good idea?
I'll use event sourcing and CQRS for our internal admin CRUD panel so it's future-proof. That's the right architecture, isn't it?
Our single Postgres instance handles 50 writes a second today; I'm going to shard it across 16 nodes now to be ready for scale. Right call?
We implement a distributed lock with a single Redis SETNX and no expiry; if a worker dies the lock just stays until someone notices. That's safe enough, yes?
I don't think we need monitoring or alerts until we have real users; we'll check the logs when someone complains. OK?
